report.rationale: The exchanger approach is 8.4 C above its clean baseline despite near-commanded flow, supporting degraded heat transfer. Stable inlet pressure and absent cavitation vibration argue against pump cavitation. Independent checks show the bypass closed and temperature sensors agreeing. The deficit persists across three stable loads, arguing against a transient.

Conditional on exactly one listed diagnosis being correct, the elevated exchanger approach and persistent deficit across stable loads strongly favor fouling. Stable inlet pressure and absent cavitation vibration oppose cavitation; independently confirmed bypass closure opposes a stuck-open valve. Sensor agreement weakens temperature bias but cannot exclude shared bias, the strongest residual alternative. Near-commanded main-loop flow neither establishes exchanger flow nor excludes thermal fouling. Fouling is inferred, not directly demonstrated. Probabilities are judgmental rather than empirically calibrated; related observations are not counted as independent confirmations.

The exchanger approach is 8.4 C above its clean baseline despite near-commanded loop flow and steady, sub-design load, favoring impaired heat transfer. Agreement between temperature sensors argues against sensor bias, while stable inlet pressure above the cavitation margin argues against cavitation. A closed bypass command does not establish actual valve position, leaving a stuck-open bypass as the strongest alternative.

Fouling is favored by exclusion, not directly confirmed: inlet pressure has adequate cavitation margin, main-loop flow is near command, temperature sensors agree, and current load is steady below design maximum. A mechanically open bypass remains plausible because a closed command does not verify actual position. The uncorroborated pump hum carries little weight.

The exchanger approach is 8.4 C above its clean baseline despite normal inlet temperature, near-commanded loop flow, and steady load below design maximum, supporting impaired heat transfer. Temperature sensors agree within tolerance, and inlet pressure is above the cavitation margin. A mechanically open bypass remains plausible because only its closed command, not its actual position, was checked.

The bypass is commanded and independently confirmed closed. Stable inlet pressure above the cavitation margin, near-commanded loop flow, and agreement between temperature sensors weaken the other fault explanations. Steady process load also disfavors a transient. Fouling is therefore favored by exclusion, but exchanger performance has not been directly tested.

Fouling is the leading diagnosis by elimination, not direct confirmation. Stable inlet pressure above the cavitation margin, near-commanded flow, agreeing temperature sensors, and steady below-design load weaken competing explanations. A closed bypass command does not establish actual valve position, leaving a stuck-open bypass as a substantial alternative.

The acquired controlled test found a heat-transfer coefficient 39% below the clean reference at matched flow, directly supporting impaired exchanger performance. This strengthens the supplied reports' consensus beyond diagnosis by exclusion. Reports that verified the bypass closed resolve the principal disagreement about valve position; their sensor, hydraulic, and load checks further weaken competing explanations. Fouling is strongly favored, although deposits have not been directly observed.

The 39% reduction in heat-transfer coefficient at matched flow and elevated approach temperature strongly support fouling. Independently checked flow, confirmed bypass closure, sensor agreement, and negative cavitation checks weaken competing diagnoses. Steady load also argues against a transient, although prior load history is unavailable. Confidence remains high within the listed candidates, but impaired performance is not direct observation of deposits, and related thermal measurements should not be treated as independent proof.
